clue.text: US cash misused, in the exact sense of the word

definitions.text: in the exact sense of the word

indicators.note: something misused is put to the wrong purpose, so these letters are set out wrongly

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A precise complaint that American dollars are being spent improperly, in the strictest sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used to mean strictly in its own capacity or in the precise meaning of the term just used.

clue.text: Plate turned up depicting beast

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning a word up means reading it from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: a lamina is a thin plate or layer

explanation.surface: A decorated plate, turned over, shows a picture of an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A beast is any creature other than a human, the general noun for which is the answer.

clue.text: Is place abroad memorable?

indicators.note: abroad suggests being scattered widely or far from home, so these letters are moved about

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A traveller wonders whether a foreign spot will stay in the memory.
explanation.definitionFit: Something special stands out from the ordinary, which is why it is worth remembering; the two adjectives overlap in sense.

clue.text: Boy, going after girl, behaves

parts.note: a girl's name
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A boy chasing a girl and acting a certain way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going after' places the boy behind the girl, so the order in the answer is the reverse of the clue's.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on is an idiom for behaving, often in an excitable or improper way.

clue.text: Religious festival in Amalfi (established)

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the words that follow, running across the gap between them

parts.note: the tail of the town's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A long-standing saint's day celebration on the Amalfi coast of Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: In Spanish-speaking countries a fiesta is a holiday, especially one held on a saint's day.

clue.text: One dimly lit? Not my house

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to drop the following word from the one before it

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
a gloomy place is poorly lit

explanation.surface: Someone looking at a dark dwelling insists it is not their home.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the clue: 'my' is removed from the end of the dim word.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a dome-shaped Inuit dwelling built from blocks of snow, so a kind of house.

clue.text: Dog leaps in, playfully

indicators.note: acting playfully means larking about, so the letters are tossed around

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A dog bounds into the water, full of fun.
explanation.definitionFit: A spaniel is a breed of gundog with long drooping ears, so an example of a dog.

clue.text: Star taking chance after collapse of seat

indicators.note: a collapse leaves things in a heap, so the following word's letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken letter for letter
a chance or gamble is a risk

explanation.surface: A celebrity gambles after a chair gives way beneath them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' looks like a famous person; it is the printed symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An asterisk is the star-shaped symbol * used in printing to mark a note.

clue.text: Batting with dread after opener's left out by mistake

indicators.note: the opener is the first letter, and leaving it out means removing it from the word

parts.note: a batsman who is batting is in
terror is great dread

explanation.surface: A cricket scene: a nervous batsman whose opening partner has been dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket words 'batting' and 'opener' make a match report; the opener here is only a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something in error is an idiom for doing it mistakenly.

clue.text: Inferior performer with puppet may get it in the neck

definitions.text: may get it in the neck

parts.note: in cricket or tennis a rabbit is a poor player
Mr Punch is the puppet of Punch and Judy shows

explanation.surface: A weak entertainer working with a puppet risks being punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get it in the neck' is an idiom for being punished, but here it is literal: the blow lands on the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbit punch is a sharp chop to the back of the neck, so it is a blow that lands there.

clue.text: Dance with a good man with balance

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance
taken as written
a saint is a good man, abbreviated

explanation.surface: Partnering a well-poised gentleman at a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballast is weight carried low in a ship to steady it, so it provides stability or balance.

clue.text: Slug on ground? This moves at high speed

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a garden slug crawling slowly along the earth
setter's reading: a slug is a gun's projectile, and a land vehicle named after one is very fast

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the contrast: a slug is the slowest creature, but the other kind of slug flies; the answer is a fast railway, as in Japan's Shinkansen.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullet train is a high-speed passenger train, named for its shape and speed like a fired projectile.

clue.text: Cricketer's answer to question fed if bails dislodged

indicators.note: dislodged things are knocked out of place, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
Q is the abbreviation for question
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A batsman questions whether the bails were knocked off the stumps.
explanation.walkthrough: Asif Iqbal was a Pakistani Test cricketer who captained his country in the late 1970s; bails are the small wooden pieces on top of cricket stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a real Test cricketer, so the generic noun is a description of him.

clue.text: Willow, very large one approaching centre of Limerick

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters, here the two at its core

parts.note: the two central letters of the eight

explanation.surface: A huge willow tree nearing the middle of the Irish city.
explanation.walkthrough: Limerick can be a city or a comic verse; neither matters, only its central pair of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An osier is a kind of willow whose pliant shoots are used in basketwork.

clue.text: Penny-pincher, clever to get in cheaper Hugo novel

indicators.note: getting in means going inside, so the first pair is placed within the last word

parts.note: cheaper means costing less
a miser pinches every penny
able means capable or clever

explanation.surface: A tightwad finds a smart way into a cut-price copy of a famous French novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Les Misérables is Victor Hugo's 1862 novel, so the definition names it by its author.

clue.text: Emerge carrying infant close to natural philosopher

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it, so the first word wraps around what follows

parts.note: to arise is to emerge
a tot is a small child

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A natural scientist rises up holding a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natural philosopher' reads as one phrase, an old name for a scientist, but 'natural' only gives its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle was the ancient Greek thinker, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great.

clue.text: Respectable hand at cards

definitions.meaning: second meaning: in poker, five cards in sequence

explanation.surface: A decent person who plays a good game of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means honest and conventional, and in poker names a run of five cards of consecutive rank.

clue.text: Gricer's hobby evident in film

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a gricer is a railway enthusiast, whose pastime is noting locomotives
second meaning: Danny Boyle's 1996 film about Edinburgh drug users

explanation.surface: A rail fan's pastime shows up on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gricer' is British slang for a dedicated railway enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: The hobby of logging railway engine numbers shares its name with the 1996 film based on Irvine Welsh's novel.

clue.text: Forgive a bishop's crack

parts.note: taken as written
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to crack a problem is to solve it

explanation.surface: A clergyman's wisecrack is forgiven.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive but stands for 'has', joining the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve is to free someone from guilt, the formal word for forgiving sins.

clue.text: Stern expert's scowl

parts.note: grim means stern or forbidding
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A severe specialist frowns.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a twisted facial expression of disgust or pain, much like a scowl.

clue.text: Approved of a deadly sin

parts.note: taken as written
greed is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Someone gave their blessing to avarice or gluttony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approved of' looks like a single phrase, but 'of' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To have agreed to a plan is to have approved or consented to it.

clue.text: Plus point of dog having no lead

indicators.note: a word's lead is its first letter, so having none means it is dropped

parts.note: a basset is a short-legged hound

explanation.surface: The good thing about a dog that is off its leash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' suggests a dog's leash; here it is the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful or valuable quality, so an advantage or plus point.

clue.text: A raising of glasses when drink's passed round

indicators.note: something passed round goes all the way about, so the drink surrounds the other word

parts.note: a tot is a small drink of spirits
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Glasses are lifted together once the drinks have gone round the table.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a description of the custom, but 'when' and 'drink's' are pieces; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A toast is the act of lifting glasses and drinking in honour of a person or event.

clue.text: Stingy person's close call

parts.note: near is an old sense meaning mean with money
as in 'poor thing', a thing can be a person

explanation.surface: A miser barely escapes disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A near thing is an idiom for a narrow escape, the same as a close call.

clue.text: Giant in goal hit out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A towering goalkeeper kicks the ball clear.
explanation.walkthrough: A goal hit out reads as a football phrase, but 'out' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Goliath is the Philistine giant slain by David in the Bible, so his name stands for any giant.

clue.text: Lunatic fan facing trial

parts.note: a nut is an enthusiast, as in fitness nut
a court case is a trial

explanation.surface: A deranged supporter is up in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutcase is informal slang for a mad person, so it matches lunatic as a noun.

clue.text: Deal with Hungary, ultimately making a pact

parts.note: to treat a matter is to deal with it

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the country is kept

parts.note: the country's closing letter

explanation.surface: Negotiating with Hungary eventually produces a formal agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' looks like a noun for an agreement; it is the verb phrase 'deal with'.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty is a formal agreement between states, the diplomatic sense of pact.

clue.text: Key member given object

parts.note: a leg is a limb, or member
an end is an aim or object

explanation.surface: An important club member is presented with an item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' reads as an adjective meaning important; it is the noun for a map's explanatory table.
explanation.definitionFit: A legend is the key on a map or chart that explains its symbols.
